questions.explain: Exact search is the honest baseline — distance to every candidate measured, true nearest neighbors returned, no index to build and 100% recall by construction.
options: It computes VECTOR_DISTANCE between the query vector and every row, sorts, and takes the top k — 100% recall, no index required
It walks a DiskANN graph touching only a small fraction of rows
It requires a CREATE VECTOR INDEX before any query can run
It returns approximate results with roughly 95% recall
questions.q: Which statement best describes exact search in SQL Server 2025?

questions.explain: The guidance is to start every vector table on exact search and promote based on production measurements — corpus size and retrieval CPU — not projections or anxiety.
options: Immediately when the table is created
When the table exceeds 1,000 rows
When production measurements show the corpus crossing roughly 50K vectors with latency pressure, or sys.dm_exec_query_stats shows retrieval CPU dominating the instance
Only after rewriting the embedding model
questions.q: According to the chapter, when should you promote a vector table from exact search to a DiskANN approximate index?

questions.explain: If you ask the index for exactly 10 candidates and a tenant filter discards 6, you return 4 — ask for 50, filter, then trim to 10; the chapter calls this the most common recall bug in production.
options: Building the DiskANN index with MAXDOP higher than the number of cores
Asking VECTOR_SEARCH for more candidates (e.g., TOP_N = 50) than the final result count (e.g., 10), because relational filters consume the candidate budget
Inserting vectors in batches of 5,000 to reduce log pressure
Querying with all three distance metrics and merging the results
questions.q: What is the 'over-fetch' pattern, and why does it matter on the approximate path?

questions.explain: HNSW is extremely fast and memory-hungry; DiskANN keeps most of the graph and full-precision vectors on disk with a bounded number of random reads per query — which is why Microsoft chose it for the in-engine index.
options: DiskANN keeps its entire graph in RAM; HNSW is SSD-backed
DiskANN guarantees 100% recall; HNSW does not
DiskANN is O(n) per query while HNSW is O(log n)
Both deliver O(log n) search at 95–99% recall, but HNSW keeps its graph in RAM while DiskANN was designed for SSDs with only a working set in memory
questions.q: How does the chapter contrast DiskANN with HNSW?

questions.explain: Recall is the fraction of the true top-k neighbors the index returns; 0.97 recall@10 means 97 of the 100 true nearest neighbors are found in milliseconds.
options: 97% of queries return in under 10 ms
The index is 97% smaller than the raw vectors
It finds 97 of the 100 true nearest neighbors in milliseconds instead of finding all 100 in over a second
97% of the vectors were indexed successfully
questions.q: A DiskANN index reports 0.97 recall@10. What does that mean?
